kcet|Chemistry|2026|7||0|0:
SN1 goes through a flat, sp² carbocation, so the nucleophile attacks equally from either face.
That only shows up as a racemic mixture if the carbon carrying the halogen is a stereocentre.
(1) (CH₃)₃CBr ionises fastest, but the product (CH₃)₃COH has two identical methyls — not chiral.
(3) (CH₃)₂CHBr and (4) CH₃Br likewise have no stereocentre.
(2) CH₃CHBrC₂H₅: that carbon holds H, CH₃, C₂H₅ and Br — four different groups, so it is chiral.
Its planar carbocation is attacked from both sides in equal measure.
∴ 2-bromobutane gives the racemic mixture.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|8||0|0.s:
Take each compound by its medicinal use.
(a) Chloramphenicol — a broad-spectrum antibiotic, the standard treatment for typhoid fever ⇒ (iv).
(b) Thyroxine — the thyroid hormone; a deficiency of it causes goitre ⇒ (iii).
(c) Chloroquine — the classic antimalarial ⇒ (i).
(d) Chloroform — once used as a general anaesthetic ⇒ (ii).
∴ a–iv, b–iii, c–i, d–ii.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|9||0|0:
The target R–CHO is the aldehyde, so the oxidation has to stop one step short of the acid.
(1) Alkaline KMnO₄ is a strong oxidant — it runs straight on to R–COOH.
(2) LiAlH₄ is a reducing agent; it works the other way.
(3) Na/C₂H₅OH is also a reducing system.
(4) PCC is Cr(VI) in a non-aqueous medium, so no hydrate forms and the oxidation halts at the aldehyde.
∴ PCC converts R–CH₂OH to R–CHO.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|10||0|0.s:
Glycerol is propane-1,2,3-triol: CH₂OH–CHOH–CH₂OH.
Classify each –OH by the carbon carrying it.
C1: the carbon bears the OH plus one other carbon ⇒ primary.
C3: identical to C1 ⇒ primary.
C2: the middle carbon bears the OH plus two carbons ⇒ secondary.
There is no carbon attached to three other carbons, so no tertiary –OH is possible.
∴ two primary and one secondary alcoholic groups.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|11||0|0.s:
The structure is (CH₃)₃C–O–C₂H₅.
In IUPAC naming an ether is an alkoxy group on the larger hydrocarbon chain.
The bigger fragment is the C(CH₃)₃ unit: as a chain that is propane, CH₃–C–CH₃.
The central carbon (C2) carries a methyl and the –OC₂H₅ group.
The –OC₂H₅ substituent is named ethoxy.
Numbering from either end puts both on C2.
∴ 2-ethoxy-2-methylpropane.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|14||0|0:
Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogen; acetophenone, C₆H₅COCH₃, does.
Dilute OH⁻ removes an α-H from the CH₃ to give the carbanion C₆H₅CO–CH₂⁻.
That carbanion adds to the carbonyl carbon of benzaldehyde — a crossed (Claisen-Schmidt) aldol.
The β-hydroxy ketone formed loses water readily because the new C=C conjugates with both rings.
The product is the chalcone C₆H₅–CH=CH–CO–C₆H₅.
∴ 'A' is the α,β-unsaturated ketone shown in option (4).

kcet|Chemistry|2026|15||0|0.s:
Acid strength is decided by how stable the anion left behind is.
A carboxylic acid gives RCOO⁻, in which the charge is shared equally by two oxygen atoms;
the two resonance forms are identical, so the delocalisation is especially effective.
Phenol gives C₆H₅O⁻, where the charge is delocalised onto ring carbon atoms —
less favourable, because carbon is far less electronegative than oxygen.
Dimer formation (1) and hydrogen bonding (2) are properties of the acid, not of its anion.
∴ because the conjugate base of a carboxylic acid is more resonance stabilised.

kcet|Chemistry|2026|16||0|0:
The iodoform test needs a CH₃–CO– group, or a CH₃–CH(OH)– group that I₂/OH⁻ can oxidise to one.
(1) Ethanal, CH₃CHO — has CH₃ next to C=O ⇒ positive.
(2) Acetone, CH₃COCH₃ — a methyl ketone ⇒ positive.
(4) Acetophenone, C₆H₅COCH₃ — also a methyl ketone ⇒ positive.
(3) Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH — the carbon beside the CH₃ is a carboxyl carbon, not a ketonic one;
in alkali it simply forms the acetate ion and is not attacked.
∴ ethanoic acid does not give the iodoform test.
